examShortTricks: Trick 1: One-line law: 'properties are a periodic function of ATOMIC NUMBER' (Moseley) — not mass; that single word earns the mark.
Trick 2: Moseley's evidence: √ν ∝ (Z − b) — X-ray frequencies depend on atomic number, not atomic mass.
Trick 3: Count blocks by last electron: s-block groups 1–2, p-block 13–18, d-block 3–12, f-block separate — draw the staircase if asked to place an element.
keyPoints: Modern periodic law: physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Moseley changed the basis from atomic mass (Mendeleev) to atomic number.
7 periods and 18 groups; s, p, d, f blocks by the subshell receiving the last electron.
practiceQuestions: Q. State the modern periodic law. How does it differ from Mendeleev's? (2 marks) — atomic number vs atomic mass as the basis.
Q. Why did Moseley correct the positions of Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I? (1 mark) — their properties depend on Z, and mass order had placed them wrongly.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Period number = shell being filled (n); group of s-block = valence electrons; group of p-block = 10 + valence electrons; d-block group = (n−1)d + ns electrons.
Trick 2: Quick placements: Na (2,8,1) → group 1 period 3; Cl (2,8,7) → group 17 period 3; Fe (2,8,14,2) → group 8 period 4.
Trick 3: Diagonal relationships (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si) come from similar ionic potentials — a favourite 1-marker.
keyPoints: Elements are arranged in 7 periods and 18 groups in increasing atomic number.
s-block: groups 1 and 2; p-block: groups 13–18; d-block: groups 3–12; f-block: lanthanides and actinides.
Group number reflects valence-shell configuration.
practiceQuestions: Q. An element has configuration 2, 8, 7. Give its period, group and block. (2 marks) — period 3, group 17, p-block (Cl).
Q. What is a diagonal relationship? Give one pair. (1 mark) — similarity of 2nd-period element with the 3rd-period element diagonally right, e.g. Li–Mg.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: IUPAC groups 1–18 numbered left to right; the old A/B sub-group labels are dropped — quote '18-group long form' as the IUPAC answer.
Trick 2: For 'why 18 groups' — the long form splits the short-form subgroups A/B and accommodates d-block elements in proper sequence.
Trick 3: f-block placement: lanthanides (Ce–Lu) and actinides (Th–Lr) are placed separately below to save width — they belong to group 3, periods 6 and 7.
keyPoints: IUPAC approves the long form with groups numbered 1 to 18.
Removes the A/B subgroup ambiguity of Mendeleev's table.
f-block elements are shown separately below the main table.
practiceQuestions: Q. How many groups and periods does the IUPAC periodic table have? (1 mark) — 18 groups, 7 periods.
Q. Where are lanthanides placed and why? (2 marks) — separately below the main table (period 6, group 3) to keep the table compact.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Zeff = Z − σ (screening constant); across a period Zeff increases (σ nearly constant) → smaller radius, higher ionization energy.
Trick 2: Down a group both Z and σ increase by the same step → Zeff stays nearly constant → size grows. This one line explains ALL group trends.
Trick 3: Slater quick value: inner electrons shield fully (σ ≈ 0.85–1 per electron) — quote 'shielding by inner shells' as the definition of σ.
keyPoints: Nuclear charge Z = number of protons; effective nuclear charge Zeff = Z − σ.
σ (sigma) is the screening effect of inner-shell electrons.
Zeff governs atomic size, ionization energy and electronegativity trends.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is Zeff of Li less than that of Be? (1 mark) — Be has one more proton with similar shielding, so Zeff is higher.
Q. Why do atomic radii increase down a group despite increasing Z? (2 marks) — new shells are added; σ increases with Z, so Zeff felt by outer electrons is nearly unchanged.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: All four trends in one sentence — across a period: radius ↓, IE ↑, EA ↑ (more negative), EN ↑; down a group: exactly the reverse.
Trick 2: Exceptions that earn marks: noble gases have NO electron affinity (stable octet); Be/N have higher IE than B/O (2s/2p stability); IE3 >> IE2 >> IE1.
Trick 3: Cation < parent atom < anion in size — compare isoelectronic series by Z: more protons → smaller (Al3+ < Mg2+ < Na+ < F− < O2− < N3−).
Trick 4: IE units — quote kJ/mol and the successive-IE jump as evidence of the shell being emptied.
keyPoints: Atomic radius decreases across a period (Zeff ↑) and increases down a group (new shells).
Ionization energy rises across a period; successive IEs always increase.
Electron affinity: energy released on adding an electron; Cl > F due to small size repulsion.
Electronegativity: tendency to attract shared pair; F is the most electronegative (4.0).
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange Na, Mg, Al in increasing ionization energy and explain the Be/B-type exception if asked. (2 marks) — Na < Mg < Al? Actually Al < Mg (3p electron easier to remove than 3s pair) — quote this exception.
Q. Why is the electron affinity of F lower than that of Cl? (2 marks) — very small F atom: added electron suffers repulsion from compact 2p shell.
Q. Arrange Al3+, Mg2+, Na+, O2−, N3− in increasing size. (2 marks) — all 10-electron species; size grows as Z falls: Al3+ < Mg2+ < Na+ < O2− < N3−.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Dipole-moment order for board exams: HF > HCl > HBr > HI (ΔEN falls) — and μ = q × d with direction from + to −.
Trick 2: % ionic character rises with ΔEN; a ΔEN ≥ 1.7 bond is taken as ionic, ≤ 0.4 as covalent — quick classification trick.
Trick 3: Bond length order: triple < double < single (C≡C < C=C < C–C); larger atoms → longer bonds (H–Cl < H–Br < H–I).
Trick 4: Zero dipole despite polar bonds = symmetric molecule (CO2, BF3, CCl4) — the vector sum cancels.
keyPoints: Bond length: equilibrium distance between nuclei of bonded atoms; decreases with higher bond order.
Dipole moment μ = charge × distance; vector from the positive to the negative end.
Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference.
Symmetric molecules with polar bonds can have μ = 0.
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange HF, HCl, HBr, HI in increasing dipole moment. (1 mark) — HI < HBr < HCl < HF.
Q. CO2 has polar bonds but zero dipole moment — why? (2 marks) — linear molecule; the two equal bond dipoles point opposite and cancel.
Q. Which is longer, C–C or C=C, and why? (1 mark) — C–C; greater s-character/bond order pulls nuclei closer.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: First law one line: m = ZIt with Z = E/96500 (E = equivalent mass) — every numerical is a direct substitution.
Trick 2: Second law in ratio form: masses deposited by the same charge are in the ratio of equivalent masses, m1/m2 = E1/E2.
Trick 3: Charge bookkeeping: Q = It (I in amperes, t in seconds); moles of electrons = Q/96500; then divide by the ion charge.
Trick 4: 1 F deposits 1 equivalent = 1 mole of electrons' worth — Ag (108 g), Cu 63.5/2, Al 27/3.
keyPoints: First law: mass deposited is proportional to the quantity of charge passed (m = ZIt).
Second law: same charge through different electrolytes deposits masses proportional to equivalent masses.
1 faraday = 96500 C = charge of 1 mole of electrons.
practiceQuestions: Q. What mass of Cu is deposited by 2 A in 30 minutes? (Cu = 63.5, Cu2+) (3 marks) — Q = 2 × 1800 = 3600 C; m = 63.5 × 3600/(2 × 96500) ≈ 1.18 g.
Q. Same current through CuSO4 and AgNO3 deposits 0.3175 g Cu. Find Ag deposited. (2 marks) — mAg = 0.3175 × (108/31.75) ≈ 1.08 g.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Quote postulates in pairs — (1) tiny molecules, huge empty space; (2) random motion, elastic collisions; (3) no attraction (ideal); (4) pressure = molecular bombardment; (5) KE ∝ T.
Trick 2: 'KE ∝ absolute temperature' is the postulate that links temperature to molecular speed — always cite it for 'why pressure rises with T'.
Trick 3: Ideal-gas behaviour follows from 'no intermolecular attraction' — real gases deviate exactly when that fails (high P, low T).
keyPoints: Gas molecules are point masses with large intermolecular spaces.
Molecular collisions are perfectly elastic; pressure arises from wall bombardment.
Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
No significant intermolecular forces in an ideal gas.
practiceQuestions: Q. State any four postulates of the kinetic theory of gases. (2 marks) — pick the four above in compact form.
Q. Why does a gas exert pressure? (1 mark) — molecules bombard the walls; rate × momentum change per collision gives pressure.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Boyle: P1V1 = P2V2 (T constant); Charles: V1/T1 = V2/T2 (P constant); combined: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 — write the one matching the 'constant' word in the question.
Trick 2: Temperatures MUST be in kelvin — convert T °C + 273 before substituting; this is the most common numerical trap.
Trick 3: Dalton: P_total = p1 + p2 + …; partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure (p_i = x_i P).
Trick 4: Aqueous tension: collected-gas problems subtract the water vapour pressure: P_dry = P_total − aq. tension.
keyPoints: Boyle's law: V ∝ 1/P at constant T.
Charles' law: V ∝ T at constant P; −273 °C is the extrapolated zero volume.
Dalton's law of partial pressures: total pressure = sum of partial pressures.
Graham's law: rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√M.
practiceQuestions: Q. A vessel holds N2 (p = 0.5 atm) and O2 (p = 0.3 atm); total pressure? (1 mark) — 0.8 atm (Dalton).
Q. O2 diffuses 4 times faster than gas X; find M_X. (2 marks) — r_O2/r_X = √(M_X/32) = 4 → M_X = 512.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: PV = nRT with R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1 when P in atm and V in litres; SI value 8.314 J K^-1 mol^-1 — pick R to match the units given.
Trick 2: Same-gas comparison: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 (n cancels); different-gas comparison: use PV = nRT and solve for the missing variable.
Trick 3: Density form: PM = dRT — molar mass from density, or density from M, in one substitution.
Trick 4: Significance of R: work done per mole per kelvin — same for ALL gases (universal).
keyPoints: Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT.
Universal gas constant has the same value for every gas.
PM = dRT links density and molar mass.
practiceQuestions: Q. 2 g of a gas occupies 1.12 L at STP. Find M. (2 marks) — n = 1.12/22.4 = 0.05; M = 2/0.05 = 40 g/mol.
Q. Find the pressure of 0.5 mol gas in 10 L at 27 °C. (2 marks) — P = nRT/V = 0.5 × 0.0821 × 300/10 = 1.23 atm.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Two causes, two directions — high pressure: molecular volume matters (V_observed > V_ideal); low temperature: attraction matters (P_observed < P_ideal).
Trick 2: Compressibility Z = PV/nRT: Z = 1 ideal, Z > 1 repulsion-dominated, Z < 1 attraction-dominated — quote Z to classify any deviation.
Trick 3: Boyle temperature: the one temperature where a real gas behaves ideally over a pressure range (Z = 1).
Trick 4: van der Waals corrections in one line: (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT — 'a' for attraction, 'b' for molecular size.
keyPoints: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT at high pressure and low temperature.
Positive deviation: repulsive forces dominate; negative: attractive forces dominate.
Compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT measures ideality.
van der Waals equation adds attraction (a) and volume (b) corrections.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why do real gases deviate at high pressure? (2 marks) — molecules occupy a finite volume; the free volume is less than V, so PV/nRT > 1.
Q. What is the compressibility factor for an ideal gas? (1 mark) — Z = 1.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Boiling point rises when vapour pressure falls — solutes, strong IMFs and external pressure all raise b.p.; quote 'VP = atmospheric pressure' as the boiling condition.
Trick 2: Vapour pressure vs temperature is exponential (Clausius) — VP always increases with T, never linearly.
Trick 3: Surface tension falls with temperature and vanishes at the critical temperature; viscosity also falls with T (opposite to gases).
Trick 4: Evaporation is surface cooling → causes condensation on a cold mirror — link evaporation, VP and b.p. in one chain.
keyPoints: Vapour pressure: pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.
Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
Surface tension and viscosity decrease with rising temperature.
Evaporation is endothermic and increases with temperature and surface area.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does water boil below 100 °C on Mount Everest? (1 mark) — lower atmospheric pressure; VP reaches it earlier.
Q. Why does salt raise the boiling point of water? (2 marks) — solute lowers vapour pressure, so a higher temperature is needed to reach 1 atm.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Two orderings define liquid crystals — positional disorder with orientational order; they flow like liquids but diffract like crystals.
Trick 2: Two classic examples: cholesteryl benzoate (thermotropic, first discovered) and soap/water mixtures (lyotropic) — name both with their class.
Trick 3: Applications list for 2 marks: LCD displays, temperature sensors (colour change), medical thermography for tumours.
keyPoints: Liquid crystals: intermediate state with liquid flow and crystal-like optical order.
Thermotropic: order changes with temperature; lyotropic: with concentration.
Used in LCDs, digital thermometers and thermal mapping of the body.
practiceQuestions: Q. What are liquid crystals? Give one example. (2 marks) — states with orientational order but liquid mobility; cholesteryl benzoate.
Q. Give two applications of liquid crystals. (1 mark) — LCD screens; colour-change thermometry.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Distinguish in one table line — crystalline: sharp m.p., anisotropic, long-range order; amorphous: range of m.p., isotropic, short-range only (glass, plastic).
Trick 2: Anisotropy is the property-based test: rotate a crystal and properties change; rotate glass and they do not.
Trick 3: Classify solids by bonding: ionic (NaCl, hard, high m.p.), molecular (ice, soft, low m.p.), covalent (diamond, hardest), metallic (Cu, conductive).
keyPoints: Crystalline solids have a regular long-range arrangement and sharp melting points.
Amorphous solids (glass) lack long-range order and melt over a range.
Crystals are anisotropic; amorphous solids are isotropic.
Four types by bonding force: ionic, molecular, covalent-network, metallic.
practiceQuestions: Q. Differentiate crystalline and amorphous solids (two points). (2 marks) — order/sharp m.p. vs disorder/melting range.
Q. Why is diamond extremely hard? (1 mark) — 3-D covalent network of sp3 carbon; every atom is bonded to four others.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: One-word trio — efflorescent: LOSE water to air (Na2CO3·10H2O); deliquescent: absorb water and DISSOLVE (CaCl2, NaOH); hygroscopic: absorb water but stay solid (silica gel).
Trick 2: Water of crystallisation count: CuSO4·5H2O (blue vitriol, 5), FeSO4·7H2O (green vitriol, 7), Na2CO3·10H2O (washing soda, 10) — quote salt + n for the 1-marker.
Trick 3: Crystal growth needs a seed crystal and a saturated solution — slow cooling gives large crystals.
keyPoints: Efflorescence: loss of water of crystallisation to the atmosphere.
Deliquescence: absorption of moisture until the solid dissolves.
Hygroscopic: absorbs moisture without dissolving.
Water of crystallisation: stoichiometric water in the crystal lattice.
practiceQuestions: Q. Classify: CaCl2, silica gel, washing soda. (2 marks) — deliquescent; hygroscopic; efflorescent.
Q. Write the formula of blue vitriol with its water of crystallisation. (1 mark) — CuSO4·5H2O.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definitions in one line each — lattice: 3-D array of points; unit cell: smallest repeating unit that builds the whole crystal by translation.
Trick 2: Seven crystal systems by edge/angle parameters (a,b,c; α,β,γ); cubic is the exam default (a = b = c, α = β = γ = 90°).
Trick 3: Atom counts per cubic cell: simple = 1 (8 × 1/8), BCC = 2 (8 × 1/8 + 1), FCC = 4 (8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2).
keyPoints: Crystal lattice: regular 3-D arrangement of points representing the pattern of particles.
Unit cell: the smallest portion which, repeated in space, generates the whole lattice.
Seven primitive crystal systems; cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic are common.
Particles per unit cell: sc = 1, bcc = 2, fcc = 4.
practiceQuestions: Q. Define unit cell with one example. (1 mark) — smallest repeating block; NaCl cubic unit cell.
Q. Calculate the number of atoms per BCC unit cell. (2 marks) — 8 corners × 1/8 + 1 body centre = 2.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: One sentence covers all shifts: the system opposes ANY imposed change — add reactant → forward; add product → backward; raise T → endothermic direction; raise P → fewer gas moles.
Trick 2: For Haber (N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, exothermic): high P, low T, remove NH3 — the standard 3-mark application.
Trick 3: Catalysts shift NOTHING — they only speed both directions equally; saying 'catalyst shifts equilibrium' loses the mark.
Trick 4: Inert gas at constant volume: no shift; at constant pressure: shifts toward more moles.
keyPoints: Le Chatelier: a system at equilibrium counteracts any change in concentration, pressure or temperature.
Increased pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction.
A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
practiceQuestions: Q. Predict the shift for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (ΔH < 0) when (a) pressure rises, (b) temperature rises. (2 marks) — (a) forward (4 → 2 moles), (b) backward (exothermic).
Q. Why does a catalyst not affect the yield of NH3? (1 mark) — it changes only the rate, not the equilibrium constant or position.
